newsitem.title: USA: Nicaraguans fear deportations from U.S..
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguans fear deportations from U.S..

text.p: Fears that U.S. immigration officials would launch a wave of deportations gripped thousands of Nicaraguan migrants in Miami on Thursday after a temporary restraining order lapsed.
A federal judge was unable to reach a decision on a preliminary injunction against deportations, the next stage in the legal process, leaving the government free to begin sending migrants home.
But U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King urged immigration officials against acting.

After listening to three hours of lawyers' arguments and faced with a pile of documents, King said it was "physically impossible" for him to make a swift decision on the injunction sought by lawyers in a class-action suit on behalf of some 40,000 Nicaraguans and other immigrants.
"It is now up to the discretion of the government as to what they do,"King said.

New immigration laws enacted in April left tens of thousands of immigrants, many of whom have lived in the United States legally for years, open to deportation to their home countries. The temporary restraining order, which by law cannot be extended further, was to expire at midnight.
After King spoke, hundreds of Nicaraguans gathered outside the courthouse howled in dismay and cried "Justice, Justice."

"It leaves us a little scared that after midnight they will start deportations. They are going to start deportations," said Nestor Nunez of the Fraternidad Nicaraguense, a community group spearheading the campaign.

Rebecca Donaire, a company supervisor, said her welder husband, Jose Bermudez, had been detained for the past 50 days in Krome Detention Centre and she was terrified he would be sent back to Nicaragua.

The couple lived in Miami, working legally but denied permanent status, for the past 10 years. "We pay our taxes. We have never asked the government for help. I just think the government doesn't want any more immigrants," she said.

Plaintiffs' attorney Ira Kurzban told the court the new laws had spread panic and fear throughout the Nicaraguan community. Children were missing school and families were moving from houses to house to avoid capture, he said.
